newsitem.title: USA: American Axle reportedly weighing buyout offer.
newsitem.headline: American Axle reportedly weighing buyout offer.

text.p: American Axle & Manufacturing Inc., a privately held auto supplier, refused to comment Monday on a published report that a New York investment group is offering to buy the firm for more than $800 million.
"There haven't been any changes in ownership. The story is speculative," said Karen Manardo, a spokesman for the Detroit-based maker of axles, driveline systems and forged products.

Crains Detroit Business reported that the Blackstone Group of New York has offered to buy the company, a major supplier to General Motors Corp.. The offer was made by David Stockman, a managing director of Blackstone. Stockman was the budget chief under former President Ronald Reagan.
Manardo would not say if American Axle is holding talks to sell the company. A representative for the Blackstone Group could not be reached for comment.
American Axle has about 8,500 employees at several facilities located in the Detroit area, Three Rivers, Mich., Buffalo and Tonawanda N.Y., and St. Catharines, Ontario.

The company had total sales in 1996 of about $2.2 billion and ranked 17th on a list of the top 150 original equipment suppliers to North America, according to Automotive News, an auto industry trade journal.

American Axle was spun off from GM in 1994 to a group of of investors led by former Chrysler Corp. manufacturing chief Richard Dauch. According to the Crains report, the buyout is designed to allow Ray Park, a Cleveland businessman and majority owner of American Axle, to cash out of his stake.

David Andrea, an analyst at Roney & Co., said a buyout may also be connected to a possible future initial public stock offering. If the company did not feel now is the right market environment, it could use a private cash infusion to upgrade plants and improve its operating performance in preparation for a future IPO.

"When you look at the largest privately held auto suppliers, American Axle is on that list," Andrea said. "It would stand to reason that in terms of capitalisation, at some point the company would be looking to tap into the public market."
